bib.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Beyond: A Comprehensive Survey on How to Make your LLMs use External Data More Wisely

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Beyond: A Comprehensive Survey on How to Make your LLMs use External Data More Wisely", Siyun Zhao, Yuqing Yang, Zilong Wang, Zhiyuan He, Luna K. Qiu, Lili Qiu (Microsoft Research Asia), arXiv:2409.14924v1, preprint, 23 Sep 2024.

COVERAGE: Read chars 0 to ~75,000 of 115,802 in full (body ends at p.18 with the Conclusion, around char 70,000). The remaining ~40k chars are references [1]-[195], skimmed only at the start and end. There is no appendix, limitations section or results table. The paper is 27 pages. Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Core taxonomy: queries split into four levels by the external data needed and the task's main focus. L1 explicit facts, L2 implicit facts, L3 interpretable rationales, L4 hidden rationales. L1-L2 focus on retrieving facts, either stated or needing basic inference. L3-L4 focus on learning and applying the rationales behind the data.
  number: none (4 levels)
  setup: conceptual framework. It is not tested empirically; the paper has no experiments.
  quote: "classifying user queries into four levels based on the type of external data required and the task's primary focus: explicit fact queries, implicit fact queries, interpretable rationale queries, and hidden rationale queries."
  where: Abstract; Sec 2.1, p.2-4
- Formalism: an application is f: Q -D-> A. Dep(q) is the minimal set of segments needed for q. An L1 query has a retriever rD(q) that closely matches Dep(q) plus an LLM generator. An L2 query decomposes into m L1 queries, with rD(q) = union of rD(qi).
  number: none
  quote: "This component ensures that rD(q) closely matches Dep(q), the minimal subset of D required to respond to q."
  where: Sec 3.1.2, p.5; Sec 4.1, p.9
- L1 (explicit facts): basic RAG is the method of choice. The paper names three challenges: data processing (multimodal content, chunking), retrieval, and evaluation (hard at component level).
  quote: "RAG [6], due to its effectiveness, flexibility, and relatively low costs, is the most commonly adopted technical solution for handling this level of queries."
  where: Sec 3.2, p.6
- Pipeline framing: RAG is "data index construction, retrieval system construction and answer generation". The IR steps are "establishing data indexes, processing queries, retrieving and matching, re-ranking, and evaluation".
  where: Sec 3.3, p.6-7
- Chunking: bigger chunks keep more coherence but carry more noise. Listed strategies are fixed-size, recursive, sliding-window, paragraph-based and semantic. Some methods pick granularity per query; others use vision models to follow document structure.
  quote: "Larger text chunks can preserve more of the semantic coherence of the context, but they also tend to contain more noise within each chunk[40]."
  where: Sec 3.3.1, p.6
- Multimodal parsing has two routes: convert to text (table-to-text, captions), or use multimodal embeddings as soft prompts.
  where: p.6
- Indexing has three types.
  - Sparse (TF-IDF, BM25): still prevalent, but it cannot recognise synonyms.
  - Dense (DPR, ANCE, SimCSE, TAS-B, Contriever, LLM2vec, Llama2Vec): includes retrievers trained on LLM feedback.
  - Hybrid: several works blend dense and sparse indexes.
  quote: "word matching methods can lead to retrieval losses due to their inability to recognize synonyms."
  where: Sec 3.3.2, p.7
- Query-document alignment has three kinds (Fig 3). Traditional alignment uses dual encoders and query rewriting. Document-domain alignment generates synthetic answers first (HyDE). Query-domain alignment generates synthetic questions per text unit and retrieves by question match [76]. SlimPLM uses a small proxy model to draft heuristic answers.
  where: p.7-8
- Re-ranking and correction: most systems rank by retriever score. Some use perplexity or perplexity gain, LLM judgment of credibility and utility, a pluggable reward-driven adapter, or a small fact-verification model that filters wrong chunks.
  where: p.7-8
- Recursive/iterative retrieval: one retrieval pass is limited in accuracy, so multiple passes fill the gaps (Kim et al. 2023 tree-like recursive retrieval with pruning; SEATER k-means tree).
  where: p.8
- Generation: LLMs are misled by irrelevant context. RAAT found that irrelevant, relevant and counterfactual noise hurt progressively more, and that fine-tuning on noisy retrievals helps. Retriever and generator can be trained jointly.
  quote: "the detrimental effects of irrelevant retrieval noise, relevant retrieval noise, and counterfactual retrieval noise on RAG models increase progressively."
  where: Sec 3.3.3, p.8
- L2 challenges: (a) adaptive retrieval volume, since a fixed top-k gives either noise or too little; (b) coordinating reasoning with retrieval. L2 solutions are iterative RAG, RAG on graph/tree, and NL2SQL.
  quote: "A fixed number of retrievals may result in either information noise or insufficient information."
  where: Sec 4.2, p.9
- Iterative RAG, planning-based: ReAct, IRCoT, RAT, GenGround. Gap-filling: ITRG, FLARE (revisits low-probability tokens), Self-RAG (learns when to search and when to stop).
  where: Sec 4.3, p.9-10
- Graph/tree RAG. KG methods: Think-on-Graph, KnowledgeNavigator, R3, Rigel-KQGA. Chunk graph/tree methods: Knowledge-Graph-Prompting (bridging, comparing and structural questions), MoGG, RAPTOR (hierarchical clustering with summaries, collapsed-tree retrieval), GraphRAG (similarity edges, community detection, per-community summaries for a global answer).
  where: Sec 4.4, p.10
- NL2SQL (e.g. Chat2DB) is advised for structured data and for queries needing "extensive data linkage".
  where: Sec 4.5, p.10-11; Conclusion
- Fine-tuning for new facts is risky. Cited work [110] says LLMs struggle to learn new facts in fine-tuning, with more hallucination. Cited work [111] says they memorise statements, and rephrasing makes the knowledge ineffective.
  quote: "Some works [ 110] have demonstrated the hardness of LLMs to acquire new factual knowledge during fine tuning."
  where: Sec 4.6, p.11
- Misclassifying the level costs quality. Treating L1 as L2 retrieves superficial, misleading material and wastes compute. Treating L2 as L1 gives too little evidence. So classify the query level before building.
  quote: "Misclassifying explicit fact queriesas implicit fact queriescan lead to the retrieval of an abundance of superficial information that is seemingly relevant but ultimately unhelpful for answering the question"
  where: Sec 4.6, p.11
- L3 (interpretable rationales) come as plain-text guidelines or structured workflows, framed as text-conditioned Moore/Mealy machines. Challenges are prompt-optimisation cost and limited interpretability. Methods: Text2MDT, MedDM, TEMPERA, RLPrompt, GrIPS, OPRO, Reflexion, CoT/ToT/GoT, Automate-CoT, and agent workflows (MetaGPT, CoML).
  where: Sec 5, p.11-13
- L4 (hidden rationales) challenges: logical retrieval, where similarity must be logical and not just semantic, and data insufficiency. Solutions: offline learning (STaR, LXS, GL, LEAP, RICP, Buffer-of-Thought, MedPrompt, Agent Hospital), in-context learning (OpenICL, vote-k, Auto-CoT, DIN-SQL, DUP), and fine-tuning (adapter, prefix, LoRA; ChatDoctor trained on 100,000 patient-doctor dialogues).
  quote: "the helpfulness of external data does not simply depend on entity-level or semantic similarity, but rather on logical congruence or thematic alignment."
  where: Sec 6.2, p.14
- In-context example retrieval: irrelevant material in the prompt distracts the LLM.
  where: Sec 6.4, p.15
- Three ways to inject domain data (Fig 6): (a) retrieve into context, (b) train a small model that guides integration, (c) fine-tune the LLM. Requirements for data, training time and compute escalate in that order. Context injection gives better interpretability and stability but is limited by the window and by "information loss in the middle" [40].
  where: Conclusion, p.17
- Practical advice: real applications mix query types, so build a routing pipeline that combines methods. For static common knowledge, use a general LLM with CoT.
  quote: "data augmented LLM applicationstypically involves a combination of diverse query types, necessitating developers to engineer a routing pipeline"
  where: p.18
- Table 1 classes datasets by level. L1: NQ, MS MARCO, TriviaQA, SQuAD, ASQA, WebQSP. L2 (multi-reference): HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle, StrategyQA, ComplexWebQuestions, WebQuestions, Mintaka, MetaQA, qasper, DROP, QuALITY, Feverous.
  where: p.5

LIMITS: The paper has no experiments, benchmarks or quantitative results. Every number above is a count or a list, and none is a measured effect. There is no limitations section. The taxonomy is the authors' proposal, with no validation that queries can be classified reliably. It is a survey from Sept 2024, so later work (reasoning models, agentic RAG, long-context models) is absent. It gives no guidance on choosing chunk sizes or top-k. Most method descriptions are one-line summaries of cited papers, so any specific method's effect needs the original paper. The "four levels" claim in the draft's source list should be attributed as a taxonomy, not a finding.

BUILDS ON: Gao et al. 2023 (RAG survey, ref [6]); Zhao et al. 2024 (RAG for AIGC survey, [7]/[10], arXiv:2402.19473, already in the note's source list); Lewis et al. (RAG, cited as [6]); HyDE [75]; Self-RAG [92]; FLARE [50]; RAPTOR [43]; GraphRAG [104]; Liu et al. "lost in the middle" [40]. Several of these arXiv IDs already appear in the note's frontmatter: 2312.10997, 2402.19473, 2310.11511, 2305.06983, 2212.10496.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.3): Main focus of the four query levels. A one-glance summary of the taxonomy.
- Fig 2 (p.4): Summary of query levels with examples.
- Fig 3 (p.8): Three types of query-document alignment. Shows traditional vs HyDE-style vs synthetic-question alignment.
- Fig 5 (p.16): Summary of main techniques per query level. This is the best figure for a lookup table of level to technique.
- Fig 6 (p.17): Three ways to inject domain data (context, small model, fine-tune).
- Fig 4 (p.12): Rationale queries (not examined beyond its caption).

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Extraction was clean. The text has some missing spaces ("queriescan"), which I left as extracted in the quotes. The figures were read from captions only; I did not view the images. The extracted full text is at /tmp/zhao.txt. The note's frontmatter already lists arXiv 2402.19473 and 2312.10997 but not 2409.14924, so a citation and references row would need adding (sharpens, not new).
